title: Mumbai Doctors Warn Oral Cancer Is Striking Patients in Their Late 20s
excerpt: Jaslok's Dr Mehul Bansali links the younger cases to tobacco and gutkha habits beginning at 12-15 — and gives the 2-3 week rule for a mouth ulcer that will not heal.
body:
• Mumbai oncologists say oral cancer is appearing in patients in their late 20s and early 30s, linked to tobacco and gutkha habits that now often begin at age 12-15.
  • Oral cavity cancer accounts for roughly 50% of head and neck cancer cases seen at Tata Memorial and Jaslok Hospital, and about 90% of oral cancers are squamous cell carcinoma, Jaslok's Dr Mehul Bansali says.
  • The warning sign to act on: a mouth ulcer or sore that does not heal within 2-3 weeks needs a specialist, not another round of home treatment.
  • A two-minute mirror self-check — feel, look and act — is the early-detection habit a separate Mumbai campaign by Dr Sewanti Limaye is urging on the city.

Oral cancer used to be a disease doctors expected in patients over 40 or 50. Mumbai specialists say that age profile is shifting down. Dr Mehul Bansali, Director of Surgical Oncology at Jaslok Hospital, says he is now seeing cancer develop in patients as young as their late 20s to early 30s, directly linked to tobacco and gutkha habits starting as early as age 12-15, often beginning in school. He recently treated a patient around 28 years old, Jaslok Hospital reports in its public health series.

Why India carries this burden

Oral cancer is the most common head and neck cancer seen in India, and it is overwhelmingly habit-driven, Bansali says: tobacco in all forms — smoking, chewing tobacco and paan — with chronic alcohol use multiplying the risk. About 90% of oral cavity cancers are squamous cell carcinoma. At Tata Memorial and Jaslok, oral cavity cancer accounts for roughly 50% of head and neck cases despite being highly preventable. A separate Mumbai awareness effort puts the wider picture similarly: Dr Sewanti Limaye of Sir H. N. Reliance Foundation Hospital notes oral cancers account for approximately 62% of head and neck cancer cases, nearly 80% of head and neck cancers are linked to tobacco, and about 25% of patients are now below 50, Medgate Today reports.

The signs, and the 2-3 week rule

Because we look inside our mouths every day, this is a cancer that can be caught early — if the signs are taken seriously. Bansali lists them: a persistent ulcer or sore that does not heal within 2-3 weeks despite treatment, a lump or growth inside the cheek or on the tongue, bad breath from infection within an ulcer, and swelling in the neck, which is typically a later sign. His guidance is specific: try local treatment for 2-3 weeks, and if the sore has not cleared, see a specialist without further delay. Diagnosis requires a biopsy, followed by CT, PET or MRI to stage the disease.

The two-minute check

Limaye's campaign, run for Head and Neck Cancer Awareness Month, asks Mumbaikars to spend two minutes to "feel, look and act" — a mirror-based self-check for early symptoms. It is the cheapest screening there is, and it matches the clinical advice: the difference between stage I-II disease, where Bansali puts the chance of survival without recurrence above 50%, and stage III-IV, where recurrence risk rises above 50% even after full treatment, is usually how long a sore was ignored.

What actually prevents it

The prevention list is unglamorous and complete: avoid tobacco and excessive alcohol entirely, start that education at school level where the habits begin, and keep routine dental check-ups, since chronic irritation from sharp or broken teeth is a minor contributing factor. Bansali is firm that patients treated for oral cancer should not return to tobacco or alcohol even occasionally. For readers in the diaspora, the habit to import is the check, not the risk: any mouth ulcer still present after three weeks, anywhere in the world, earns a specialist appointment.
